sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. 2010. The Kháng language of Vietnam in comparison to Ksingmul (Xinh-mun). In K. A. McElhanon & G. Reesink (eds.), A Mosaic of languages and cultures: studies celebrating the career of Karl J. Franklin, 138-154. SIL e-Books 19. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No Kháng-specific stress statement. §1 has only the family-level remark that Mon-Khmer word shapes are 'weak-syllable (with reduction of vocalic and prosodic features) + strong-syllable'; §2-2.1 say Kháng 'shows only vestiges of the original sesquisyllabic pattern' (ʔbu./sa./ma. presyllables in animal and nature words); §3 'Kháng/Bumang syllables and tone' describes six tones with F0 plots. Than Uyên (Lai Châu) variety; Bumang data from Dao Jie.

sources.citation: Tạ Quang Tùng. 2021. A Phonology and Lexicon of Khang in Vietnam. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (JSEALS) 14.2: i-xxix. hdl:10524/52487 (CC-BY).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing: the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur. §3 gives the word template (C1ə̌/ǎ).C2(C3)V(C4)T, says 99.45% of the 917-item lexicon is monosyllabic and only five words have a presyllable (with extra-short /ə̌/ or /ǎ/); §6 describes eight lexical tones (six on sonorant-final, two on stop-final syllables) plus voice-register correlates. Nam Mu village variety (Tuần Giáo, Điện Biên).
